topics.title: 1.8.3 Public Goods, Private Goods and Quasi-Public Goods
1.8.4 Positive and Negative Externalities in Consumption and Production

cards.back: Bounded rationality — the idea that individuals are limited in their ability to make rational decisions due to a lack of information, time or ability to process information.

Bounded self-control — the idea that individuals may not always act in their own best interests due to a lack of self control.

Example: knowing a gym habit pays off but failing to keep it — the reasoning behind commitment devices.

Anchoring bias — the idea that individuals may be influenced by the first piece of information they receive when making a decision, even if it is not relevant or accurate.

Example: a £100 product discounted to £80 reads as a bargain, judged against the anchor rather than rivals' prices.

cards.front: Name the other behavioural biases in AQA's specification, beyond anchoring.
cards.back:
• Availability bias — judging by the information that comes to mind most easily.
  • Framing bias — swayed by how information is presented ('90% fat free' vs '10% fat').
  • Herding (social norms) — following others' choices rather than deciding independently.
  • Rules of thumb — habitual shortcuts that save effort but can miss better options.
  • Altruism — choices made to benefit others, not to maximise own utility.

Nudges — a concept in behavioural economics that refers to subtle interventions or changes in the choice architecture that influence people's behaviour in a predictable way without restricting their freedom of choice.

cards.front: Give a real-world example of a nudge used in UK economic policy.
cards.back:
Workplace pension auto-enrolment (rolled out from 2012): the default was switched from opt-in to opt-out. Freedom of choice was untouched, but participation among eligible private-sector employees roughly doubled to nearly nine in ten.

Application point: changing the default exploited inertia — a textbook nudge working at national scale.

Partial market failure — the market provides the good, but in the wrong quantity: merit goods are under-provided, demerit goods over-provided.

Complete market failure — when the market fails to provide a good or service at all e.g. public goods like national defence or street lighting: a missing market.

A quasi-public good has some but not all of the characteristics of a public good — it is partially non-excludable or partially non-rival.

Examples: roads (excludable via tolls, rival when congested) and beaches. AQA expects you to place goods on the spectrum rather than in boxes.

cards.front: Define common pool resources, and the problem they suffer.
cards.back:
Common pool resources — natural resources that are non-excludable but rivalrous, such as fish in the ocean or grazing land.

Because no one can be excluded but each use depletes the stock, they are over-exploited — the tragedy of the commons.

cards.front: Draw the welfare loss caused by a negative production externality.
cards.back: Producers face only their private costs, so external costs are ignored and MSC lies above MPC. The market produces at Q1, where MPC = MPB, but the social optimum is Q2, where MSC = MSB. The shaded triangle between the two is the welfare loss from over-production.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSC above S equals MPC and D equals MPB equals MSB, showing market output Q1 beyond the social optimum Q2 and a shaded welfare loss triangle

cards.front: Draw the welfare loss caused by a positive consumption externality.
cards.back: Consumers count only their private benefits, so MSB lies above D=MPB. The market consumes at Q1, where MPB = MPC, but the social optimum is Q2, where MSB = MSC. The shaded triangle is the welfare loss from under-consumption.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSB above D equals MPB and S equals MPC equals MSC, showing market output Q1 below the social optimum Q2 and a shaded welfare loss triangle

cards.back: Merit goods — goods that exhibit positive externalities in their consumption or production, and are therefore under-provided by the market. Examples include education, healthcare, and public libraries.
Demerit goods — goods that exhibit negative externalities in their consumption or production, and are therefore over-provided by the market. Examples include tobacco, alcohol, and sugary food.
